goal.title: Explain water movement and gas exchange in plants
goal.currentLevel: I know the basic roles of roots, xylem, and stomata, and want to connect those structures to how plants respond to their environment.
goal.focusAreas: Apply water-potential gradients, transpiration, and stomatal regulation to observations and environmental changes. Explain tradeoffs between carbon dioxide uptake and water loss.

sourceDocuments.name: Plant water transport: selective study notes
sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective study notes, checked 2026-09-10; not a quotation or complete page. Reference: https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/30-5-transport-of-water-and-solutes-in-plants

Net water movement follows a gradient from higher to lower total water potential. Solute concentration and pressure contribute to that total; knowing one component alone need not determine the total gradient. Evaporation from leaves creates tension that helps pull water through xylem, with water cohesion and adhesion helping sustain the column. The leaf-to-air vapor gradient influences transpiration. At otherwise matching temperatures, higher atmospheric humidity reduces that gradient. Guard cells regulate stomatal openings in response to environmental and internal signals. Open stomata permit carbon dioxide exchange but also provide a route for water-vapor loss. Restricting stomatal opening therefore involves a tradeoff between carbon dioxide entry and water conservation. Leaf water status, light, and carbon dioxide can affect stomatal behavior; a change in one environmental factor does not establish a fixed rate for every plant. These notes give general mechanisms, not measurements for any particular plant or experiment.

items.prompt: A plant physiologist exposes a well-watered plant to bright light while gradually raising ambient CO₂ concentration. Stomata begin partially closed at elevated CO₂. Which tradeoff shifts as a result of this response?
choices: Increased water loss is traded for higher carbon dioxide uptake.
Photosynthesis stops completely to maximize water conservation.
Carbon dioxide uptake becomes unlimited while water loss is eliminated.
Reduced water loss is traded for continued adequate carbon dioxide uptake.

goal.title: Read conditions and exceptions accurately in English
goal.currentLevel: I read everyday English comfortably but sometimes misunderstand qualifications in instructions and emails.
goal.focusAreas: Interpret conditions, exceptions, negation, and modal verbs in short instructions or correspondence. Compare paraphrases and conclusions while preserving what the text actually commits the writer to.

items.prompt: Email: "We can reschedule your appointment if you notify us at least 48 hours in advance and no staff shortages exist; otherwise, rescheduling is not guaranteed." The recipient notifies 72 hours in advance during a staff shortage. What does the email commit to?
choices: The email commits to nothing specific.
Rescheduling is guaranteed.
Rescheduling is not guaranteed.
Rescheduling is permitted but requires manager approval.

items.prompt: Notice: "Access will be revoked if either (a) credentials are shared, or (b) login attempts from unrecognized locations exceed three, unless the user has pre-registered those locations." User Z shared credentials and had four unrecognized logins without pre-registration. What does the notice commit to?
choices: Access may be revoked pending review.
Access will not be revoked due to the location exception.
The notice is silent on this combination of facts.
Access will be revoked.

Water will move from Cell A to Cell B.
Water will move from Cell B to Cell A.

goal.title: Understand sound intensity and decibels for audio work
goal.currentLevel: I can work with ratios and logarithms, but confuse changes in sound pressure, intensity, and decibel level.
goal.focusAreas: Apply sound intensity and decibel relationships to comparisons with several changes or constraints. Interpret the physical quantities and assumptions behind sound-level measurements.

sourceDocuments.name: Sound intensity and level: selective study notes
sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective study notes, checked 2026-09-10; not a quotation or complete page. Reference: https://openstax.org/books/physics/pages/14-2-sound-intensity-and-sound-level

Intensity measures sound power crossing a unit area: I = P/A, in W/m². For the sinusoidal sound-wave model, pressure amplitude Δp gives I = (Δp)²/(2ρv), where ρ is medium density and v is sound speed. Thus intensity scales with squared pressure amplitude when the medium is unchanged. Sound intensity level is β = 10 log10(I/I₀), using I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m² as the reference. Subtracting two levels with the same reference gives 10 log10(I₂/I₁). A tenfold intensity ratio corresponds to 10 dB; doubling intensity adds approximately 3.01 dB. Intensity, pressure amplitude, and logarithmic level are different quantities. A ratio of intensities determines a level difference without determining either absolute level. These notes concern physical sound quantities; an equipment dial or perceived loudness is not automatically an intensity measurement.

items.prompt: A microphone datasheet states sensitivity: –40 dBV/Pa at 1 kHz. An engineer measures 0.1 V output from this mic in a different sound field. What additional information is needed to find the sound pressure level in dB SPL?
choices: The atmospheric temperature during measurement.
The impedance of the recording interface.
The frequency of the measured sound to verify sensitivity applies.
The microphone's self-noise floor in dB SPL.

items.prompt: A mixing engineer compares two sine-wave tones in air at 20 °C. Tone A has pressure amplitude 2.0 Pa; tone B has amplitude 4.0 Pa. The engineer calculates that B is 6 dB louder than A. A colleague claims this comparison is invalid because the calculation ignores air density and sound speed. Is the colleague correct?
choices: Yes; the decibel difference depends on frequency, not just pressure amplitude.
No; the comparison is valid because the medium is identical for both tones.
Yes; the absolute intensity values require knowing ρ and v to compute.
No; but only because the ratio happens to be a perfect square.

items.prompt: A student observes that a potted wilting plant recovers turgidity within hours after watering, even though the soil was dry. Which mechanism best explains how water reached the leaf cells so quickly?
choices: Phloem transported water from storage tissues to leaves.
Tension in the xylem from transpiration pulled water upward as soil water became available.
Root pressure pushed water rapidly to the leaves.
Osmosis directly from soil to leaf cells without vascular tissue.

items.prompt: A tone has pressure amplitude 1.0 Pa in air at 20 °C. In water at the same temperature, a tone with identical pressure amplitude is produced. How does the sound intensity level in water compare to that in air?
choices: Lower, because water's higher ρv reduces intensity for the same pressure amplitude.
Equal, because pressure amplitude determines level directly.
Higher, because water's incompressibility increases pressure effects.
Higher, because water transmits sound more efficiently.

Species N has higher photosynthetic efficiency that requires less CO₂.
Both species will show identical growth rates under all conditions.
